title: Flatbreads
subtitle: quick yoghurt flatbreads cooked in a dry pan
excerpt: These flatbreads require no yeast and no proving time. Greek yoghurt gives the dough a little tang and keeps the texture soft. Cook them in a hot dry pan for a few minutes each side and eat them while warm.
sourceNotes: Yoghurt flatbreads are common across South Asian and Middle Eastern baking traditions. This is a simplified home version.

recipe.freezeNotes: Stack with baking paper between each. Reheat in a dry pan from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept covered at room temperature.
recipe.temperatureNote: Stovetop -- medium-high heat in a dry frying pan

content.text: Roll the flatbreads thin -- about 3mm. If they are too thick they will be doughy in the middle. You want to see bubbles forming on the surface when the first side is done, which is the cue to flip.

items.prepNote: use 1 tbsp vegetable oil -- for a vegan version, replace yoghurt with plant-based yoghurt and omit

content.text: Combine the flour, baking powder, and salt. Add the yoghurt and mix to a soft, non-sticky dough. If it is dry, add a tablespoon of water at a time. If too sticky, add a little more flour.
Knead briefly for 2 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 15 minutes. This relaxes the gluten and makes rolling much easier.
Divide into 8 equal pieces. On a lightly floured surface, roll each piece into a thin oval or round, about 3mm thick.
Heat a dry frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook each flatbread for 2 minutes until bubbles appear and the underside is charred in spots. Flip and cook for another 1 to 2 minutes.
Stack the cooked flatbreads under a clean cloth to keep them soft while you cook the rest. Serve warm.

items.cause: Rolled too thin, or cooked on too high a heat.
items.fix: 3mm is the target thickness. The pan should be hot but not scorching -- you want char spots, not incineration.

items.symptom: Dough is too sticky to roll
items.cause: Yoghurt varies in thickness between brands.
items.fix: Add flour a tablespoon at a time until the dough stops sticking to your hands.

content.text: Flatbreads in one form or another appear in virtually every food culture. This quick yoghurt version is most closely related to South Asian roti traditions, though the method is now widely used in home kitchens across Britain. They are endlessly versatile -- serve alongside curry, as a wrap, with dips, or simply warm with butter.
